questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Explain how the main memory is used during the machine cycle. (2 marks)

(b) State two ways of improving the performance of a CPU. (2 marks)

(c) What is an embedded system? (1 mark)

(d) Describe two uses of an embedded system. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Main memory and the machine cycle (2 marks).** The main memory (RAM) holds the program instructions and the data that are being processed. In the *fetch* stage the CPU puts the address of the next instruction (kept in the program counter) on the address bus, and the instruction is copied from that main-memory location into the CPU. In the *decode* and *execute* stages the CPU may read data (operands) from main memory, or write the result of the operation back to main memory, before the cycle starts again with the next instruction.

**(b) Improving CPU performance (2 marks)** (any two):

- Increase the clock speed (more cycles per second).
- Use a multi-core processor, so that several instructions are executed at the same time.
- Increase the size of the cache memory, so that the CPU waits less for the slower RAM.
- Use a larger word length and wider buses (more bits processed and transferred at a time), or more and faster RAM.

**(c) Embedded system (1 mark).** A small computer system (a microprocessor with memory and input/output) built into a larger device or machine to carry out one dedicated function, usually without the user being able to reprogram it.

**(d) Two uses (2 marks)** (any two):

- In domestic appliances: the controller of a washing machine or a microwave oven sets the programme, time and temperature.
- In vehicles: engine management, anti-lock braking and air-bag systems.
- In traffic lights, digital cameras, watches, ATMs or medical devices such as a pacemaker.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Using diagrams, differentiate between bus topology and mesh topology. (4 marks)

(b) What is fault tolerance of a network? (1 mark)

(c) Between bus topology and mesh topology, which is more fault tolerant? Give reasons for your answer. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Bus topology and mesh topology (4 marks).**

*Bus topology:* all the devices are connected to one common cable (the backbone), with a terminator at each end.

```
 [PC 1]    [PC 2]    [PC 3]    [PC 4]
   |         |         |         |
===+=========+=========+=========+===   backbone cable
|T|                                 |T|   (T = terminator)
```

*Mesh topology:* every device is connected directly to every other device (full mesh), or to several others (partial mesh).

```
 [A] ------------- [B]
  |  \           /  |
  |    \       /    |
  |      \   /      |
  |        X        |
  |      /   \      |
  |    /       \    |
 [D] ------------- [C]
```

Differences:

- A bus uses a single shared cable, so it is cheap and easy to install, but all the data travel on the same cable, collisions are frequent and performance drops as devices are added; a mesh uses many links (n(n-1)/2 for n devices), so it is expensive and hard to install, but each link carries only its own traffic and gives high speed.
- In a bus, if the backbone breaks the network is split or stops completely; in a mesh the data can use another route when one link fails.

**(b) Fault tolerance (1 mark).** The ability of a network to keep working (possibly with reduced performance) when one of its components, such as a cable, a node or a device, fails.

**(c) More fault tolerant (2 marks).** The **mesh topology**. There are several alternative paths between any two devices, so when one cable or node fails the data are re-routed through another path and the rest of the network continues to work. In a bus topology there is only one backbone: a single break in it (or a faulty terminator) stops communication for all the devices.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following data security measures.

(a) Data integrity. (1 mark)

(b) Data confidentiality. (1 mark)

(c) Data encryption. (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Data integrity (1 mark).** The accuracy, completeness and consistency of data throughout their life: the data are not altered, damaged or destroyed, by accident or by an unauthorised person.

**(b) Data confidentiality (1 mark).** Keeping data secret: only authorised persons are allowed to see or use the data (by passwords, access rights, encryption).

**(c) Data encryption (1 mark).** The conversion of data (plain text) into an unreadable form (cipher text) by an algorithm and a key, so that only a person who holds the right key can decrypt and read it.
